items.passage:
"Read it again," Akari said, the mayor's paper folding in her glove.
Each evening on the Riga platform, Kalani, the town's only doctor,
had copied the notice into three languages, slowly,
checking every verb against the old dictionary she carried.
Tonight the train was late; the lamps hummed above the tracks.
Akari pointed to one line: her word for "closed"
had become "abandoned" in the version already pasted on the station wall.
Kalani was ______ by the error.
She did not argue or apologize.
She took a pencil from her coat, crossed out the word on the posted sheet,
and wrote the smaller word above it, letter by letter,
while the arriving train drowned whatever Akari said next.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: openly embarrassed
mildly amused
slowly distracted
quietly troubled
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Kalani는 매일 저녁 모든 동사를 사전과 대조할 만큼 번역의 정확성에 마음을 쓰는 인물로 그려지므로 오류에 무심할 수 없다. 뒷부분에서 그녀는 따지지도 사과하지도 않고 연필로 한 글자씩 조용히 고쳐 쓰므로, 반응의 정도는 겉으로 드러나지 않는 차분한 동요여야 한다. 두 조건을 모두 만족하는 것은 D이다. A는 오류에 신경 쓴다는 점은 맞지만 드러내 놓고 당황한다는 정도가 뒤의 침착한 행동과 어긋나고, B는 정확성에 대한 그녀의 집착과 맞지 않으며, C는 지문의 'slowly'를 빌렸을 뿐 오류 앞에서의 반응을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: When I worked nights on the ward, I passed a clock-maker's shop in Ohio every morning, and Hedwig was always already at his bench, tightening the same brass wheel of the same tall clock. Winifred, my patient in bed four, had sent it there. Every week she asked whether it was ready, and every week I said soon. One morning Hedwig set down his loupe and told me the clock would never keep time again; the case had warped. I carried that sentence back to the ward like a cold cup of tea. Winifred, though, was ______ when I repeated it. She asked me to tell Hedwig to keep working on it anyway, and that night she wound her small wristwatch twice before sleeping, holding it near her ear.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: calmly accepting
openly distressed
coldly dismissive
mildly relieved
items.explanation: Winifred는 매주 시계가 준비됐는지 묻는데, 이는 수리의 완성보다 수리가 계속되는 과정 자체에 마음을 두고 있음을 보여 준다. 고칠 수 없다는 말을 들은 뒤에도 그녀는 계속 작업해 달라고 부탁하고 손목시계를 태엽 감아 귀에 대므로 반응은 동요 없이 받아들이는 쪽이다. 따라서 A가 두 단서를 모두 만족한다. B는 시계에 대한 애착만 보고 고른 표현으로 뒤의 차분한 부탁과 맞지 않고, C는 지문의 'cold'를 빌린 표현으로 계속 고쳐 달라는 부탁과 어긋나며, D는 안도할 이유가 지문에 없다.

items.passage: Coins rattled in Savitri's palm as she counted them a second time at the ticket window of the Accra depot. She did this every trip, my stepmother, recounting fares she had already counted at home, as if the numbers might change on the way over. I was fifteen and certain she did it to look busy. That afternoon the clerk said the Kumasi coach had left an hour earlier; she had read the timetable wrong. I waited for her to blame the board, or the clerk, or me. Instead she was ______ about it. She bought two cold sodas with part of the fare money, sat beside me on the bench, and asked me, of all people, to read the next departure aloud.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: visibly flustered
unexpectedly frank
politely evasive
busily occupied
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Savitri가 요금을 거듭 세는 습관은 실수를 두려워하는 사람처럼 보이게 하고, 화자는 그녀가 남 탓을 하리라 예상한다. 그러나 뒤에서 그녀는 자기 실수를 감추지 않고 화자 옆에 앉아 다음 출발 시각을 읽어 달라고 부탁하므로, 실수를 숨김없이 인정하는 태도가 드러난다. 따라서 B가 '예상과 달리'라는 의외성과 솔직함을 모두 담는다. A는 앞의 습관과만 맞고 뒤의 여유 있는 행동과 어긋나며, C는 도움을 청하는 행동과 맞지 않고, D는 지문의 'busy'를 빌린 표현일 뿐이다.

items.passage: Rope creaked against the pilings, and the smell of diesel and wet pine hung over the dock at Marseille. Saga, the coach, had brought two coffees and set one on the post beside Mathis without a word. She went through the season in neat, careful sentences: the three home losses, the missed rotation in March, the injury report she had filed in triplicate, the scouts who had stopped calling by May. She named each match by its date. She thanked him for his patience on the bench. Mathis watched a gull work at a bread crust and did not reach for the cup. Saga stopped listing. She looked at the water for a while. "You could have played the last game," she said. "I knew that then." Mathis kept watching the gull. Saga picked up his coffee, still full and long gone cold, poured it into the lake, and refilled the cup from her own.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: It shifts from a formal accounting of the season to a personal admission, in response to Mathis's withholding.
It shifts from grateful politeness to a cooler formality, in response to Mathis's lack of thanks.
It shifts from a formal accounting of the season to a personal admission, in response to Saga's memory of March.
It shifts from a formal accounting of the season to a sharp rebuke, in response to Mathis's withholding.
items.explanation: 앞부분의 Saga는 날짜와 기록을 촘촘히 나열하며 공식적인 시즌 보고를 하지만, 목록을 멈춘 뒤에는 짧은 문장으로 마지막 경기를 뛰게 할 수 있었다는 개인적 인정을 한다. 그 전환 사이에 Mathis는 커피에 손대지 않고 갈매기만 보며 반응을 보이지 않는데, 마지막에 Saga가 식은 커피를 버리고 자기 것을 따라 주는 동작은 그의 침묵에 다가가려는 반응으로 읽힌다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 겉의 정중함만 보고 변화를 잘못 읽었고, C는 전환의 원인을 Saga 자신의 기억으로 뒤집었으며, D는 인정을 질책으로 한 단계 과장했다.

items.passage: I had known Haneul for eleven years before he asked me to help him keep a promise. He was a retired sailor, and he spoke of knots, tides, and the weight of anchor chain with the patience of a man reciting prayers. On the terrace that evening above Busan he laid out the plan in order: the paper boat for Younghee's small daughter, the coat of candle wax, the exact harbor stairs where she would launch it at dawn on Sunday, the hour the tide would turn. He drew the stairs on a napkin. I nodded at each step. Then I told him what Younghee had told me that morning, that the family was moving to Seoul on Friday. Haneul folded the napkin once. He asked whether the persimmons on my side of the wall were ripe yet, and whether I had enough put away for winter. Then he took a second napkin from the stack and began, carefully, to draw the stairs again, this time with Friday's tide table beside them.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: It shifts from instructive seriousness to relaxed small talk, as Haneul tires of explaining the plan.
It shifts from confident planning to a guarded deflection, as Haneul takes in news that threatens his promise.
It shifts from confident planning to a guarded deflection, as Haneul doubts the plan he has drawn himself.
It shifts from confident planning to open despair, as Haneul takes in news that threatens his promise.
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Haneul은 종이배 계획을 순서대로 자세히 설명하지만, 아이의 가족이 금요일에 떠난다는 소식을 들은 뒤 냅킨을 접고 감나무 이야기로 화제를 돌린다. 마지막에 금요일 물때표를 곁들여 계단을 다시 그리는 동작은 그 화제 전환이 포기가 아니라 약속을 위협하는 소식을 소화하는 방식이었음을 보여 준다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A는 화제 전환을 겉으로 보이는 가벼운 잡담으로만 읽었고, C는 원인을 Haneul 자신의 계획에 대한 의심으로 뒤집었으며, D는 정도를 절망으로 과장해 다시 계획을 세우는 행동을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage:
By the ninth week of the dry season
Ama had taught Zainab every jar:
millet tied with red thread, cowpea with blue,
okra wrapped in newsprint from the year of floods,
each lid tapped twice, each name said aloud.
Zainab learned the counting and the drying racks,
the way a seed is tested in a cup of water,
the floaters tossed out, the sinkers kept.
She spoke of the bus to the coast,
of cousins, of work in the port.
Ama kept sorting.
Then Ama stopped naming.
She let a full jar stand open in the light.
At dusk she pressed a twist of cloth, unlabeled,
into the girl's hand,
and turned back to the shelves
before Zainab could untie it.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: It shifts from lively instruction to weary routine, as the elder grows tired of naming every jar.
It shifts from exacting instruction to a quiet release, as the elder doubts her own skill as a teacher.
It shifts from exacting instruction to a quiet release, as the elder comes to terms with the apprentice's plans.
It shifts from exacting instruction to a grieving protest, as the elder resists the apprentice's plans.
items.explanation: 시의 앞부분은 실 색깔, 포장지, 뚜껑 두드리기까지 세세하게 나열하며 Ama의 엄격한 가르침을 보여 주지만, Zainab이 해안행 버스와 항구 일을 말한 뒤 행이 짧아지고 Ama는 이름 부르기를 멈춘다. 마지막에 이름표 없는 씨앗 꾸러미를 건네고 돌아서는 동작은 떠나려는 제자의 뜻을 받아들이고 보내 주는 마음으로 읽힌다. 따라서 C가 정답이다. A는 짧아진 행을 단순한 피로로 읽었고, B는 원인을 Ama 자신의 자질에 대한 의심으로 뒤집었으며, D는 선물을 건네는 행동과 맞지 않게 정도를 항의로 과장했다.

items.passage: Four rules governed my kite yard on the plateau: spruce for the spars, never pine; glue only in still air; tissue cut a finger wider than the frame; no kite leaves the yard unfinished. I conducted the youth orchestra in town, and for two summers Elan, my youngest violinist, came on Saturdays to build one kite with me. We measured, argued over tail length, and logged each step in a notebook his mother, Nayeli, had given him. In August his family moved to Phoenix. For a while I kept explaining the rules to the empty bench. Then I stopped writing in the notebook. The frame still leaned against the shed wall, its skin half on. Last week a package came with a rehearsal recording; Elan plays the slow movement, a little sharp. I listened twice. Then I lifted the frame from the wall and set it, as it was, on the shed roof to face the wind.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: It shifts from cheerful instruction to lasting gloom, as the narrator gives up on building kites.
It shifts from rule-bound precision to a looser acceptance, as the narrator tires of keeping the notebook.
It shifts from rule-bound precision to a bitter regret, as a recording from Elan reaches the narrator.
It shifts from rule-bound precision to a looser acceptance, as a recording from Elan reaches the narrator.
items.explanation: 글은 연 만들기의 규칙 네 가지를 정밀하게 나열하며 시작하지만, Elan이 떠난 뒤 문장이 짧아지고 노트 기록도 멈춘다. 마지막에 화자는 Elan의 연습 녹음을 두 번 듣고 나서 미완성 연을 그대로 지붕에 올려 바람을 맞히는데, 이는 '미완성 연은 마당을 떠나지 않는다'는 자기 규칙을 내려놓는 행동이다. 따라서 규칙에서 수용으로의 전환과 그 계기를 함께 말한 D가 정답이다. A는 짧아진 문장을 체념으로만 읽었고, B는 원인을 화자 자신의 피로로 뒤집었으며, C는 방향은 비슷하나 정도를 쓰라린 후회로 과장했다.

items.passage: Rafaela had been my teacher for four years, and she had failed me in the last one. Thirty years later, at the grape harvest outside Porto Alegre, we were assigned the same row. She worked the way she had once graded: she clipped each bunch at the knuckle, turned it to check for rot, sorted the split grapes into a separate pail, and corrected the angle of my shears twice without looking up. I said little. Around ten, Danish, the foreman, came by with water and mentioned that she had asked to be put on my row. Rafaela kept clipping. Her bunches came more slowly after that, and some went into the basket unturned. Near noon she reached across and took the heavier crate from my side, carried it to the cart herself, and did not come back for her shears.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: It moves from exacting correction to a halting gentleness, after the foreman reveals Rafaela's request.
It moves from exacting correction to weary carelessness, after the long morning of work tires Rafaela.
It moves from exacting correction to a halting gentleness, after the narrator's silence unsettles Rafaela.
It moves from exacting correction to an open remorse, after the foreman reveals Rafaela's request.
items.explanation: 앞부분의 Rafaela는 송이를 하나하나 확인하고 화자의 가위 각도까지 고쳐 주는 엄격한 모습이지만, 감독 Danish가 그녀가 일부러 화자의 줄을 요청했다고 말한 뒤 작업이 느려지고 확인 없이 넣는 송이가 생긴다. 마지막에 화자 쪽의 무거운 상자를 대신 옮기고 가위를 두고 가는 동작은 숨겨 온 의도가 드러난 뒤의 서툰 다정함으로 읽힌다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 느려진 작업을 겉으로 보이는 피로로만 읽었고, C는 원인을 화자의 침묵으로 바꾸었으며, D는 말 없는 행동을 드러난 후회로 한 단계 과장했다.

items.passage: Seun bought fish on Thursdays. He walked out past the salt flats east of Havana, where the white crust cracked under his sandals, to the shack where Dario laid the morning catch on wet sacking. Each week Dario wrapped Seun's two snappers in newspaper and, without comment, tucked in a third, smaller fish. Seun assumed it was one too small to sell and thanked him in the polite voice his mother had taught him. This Thursday, Dario counted the coins and slid half of them back across the sacking. He said he had spoken to Seun's mother; from now on Seun would mend nets on Saturdays instead of paying, and the third fish had been an advance on that work for months. Seun looked at the newspaper bundle. Nobody had asked him. He held the coins a long time. Then he set them down on the sacking, picked up only two of the fish, and walked back across the salt without saying whether he would come on Saturday.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It begins with Seun's weekly errand, then lingers on the details of Dario's catch, and ends by returning to that errand.
It begins with a repeated small gesture, then presents a revelation that recasts that gesture, and ends with an undecided response.
It begins with a revelation about an arrangement, then recalls the gesture that came before it, and ends with an undecided response.
It begins with a repeated small gesture, then presents a revelation that recasts that gesture, and ends by settling Seun's doubts.
items.explanation: 지문은 Dario가 매주 말없이 작은 생선 한 마리를 더 넣어 주는 몸짓과 이를 선물로 여긴 Seun의 인식을 먼저 보여 준다. 이어 Dario가 그 생선이 Seun의 어머니와 정한 노동의 선불이었다고 밝히면서 앞의 몸짓이 다시 읽히고, Seun은 토요일에 올지 말하지 않은 채 떠나 결말이 열려 있다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A는 전반부 장면만 구조로 요약했고, C는 실제 전개 순서를 뒤집었으며, D는 열린 결말을 의심이 해소된 결론으로 잘못 읽었다.

items.passage: Who pays rent by money order anymore? Adaeze did, every first of the month, standing in line at the little post office outside Albuquerque with her slip already filled out in block capitals. Waya, who owned her building and also, by chance, worked the counter on Mondays, stamped each one and slid it into the drawer he kept for his own mail. For six years he had noticed that she never asked for a receipt. He took it as trust, and it pleased him in a way he mentioned to no one. In March she arrived without a slip. She asked whether he still had the receipts she had never requested, because she was applying for a loan and the bank wanted proof of every payment. Waya opened the drawer. The money orders were there, all seventy-two, uncashed; he had meant to deposit them in batches and kept putting it off. Adaeze looked at the stack. Behind her, someone in line coughed. Waya picked up the stamp, set it down, and reached for a pen.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It begins with a question about paying rent, then describes a long monthly routine, and ends by recalling those earlier years.
It begins with a request that exposes a problem, then traces the routine that caused it, and ends before either character fully responds.
It begins with a routine that one character reads as trust, then shows a request that recasts that routine, and ends before either character fully responds.
It begins with a routine that one character reads as trust, then shows a request that recasts that routine, and ends by resolving the matter of the payments.
items.explanation: 지문은 Adaeze가 영수증을 한 번도 요구하지 않은 습관을 Waya가 신뢰로 받아들였다는 데서 시작한다. 그런데 대출 때문에 모든 납부 증빙이 필요하다는 그녀의 요청과 서랍 속 현금화되지 않은 72장의 우편환이 그 습관을 다시 보게 만들고, Waya가 펜에 손을 뻗는 데서 두 사람의 반응이 끝나지 않은 채 멈춘다. 따라서 C가 정답이다. A는 도입부의 습관만 요약했고, B는 요청과 습관의 순서를 뒤집었으며, D는 열린 결말을 문제가 해결된 것으로 잘못 읽었다.

items.passage: Smoke and wax and the low hum of forty hives: that is how my yard in Dhaka smelled the summer my son Lucius stopped speaking to me. On our lane, every keeper closed the hives at noon on Fridays because Sharda, who had kept bees longest, said the colonies needed the rest. No one believed it. Everyone obeyed. Lucius, fourteen, left our lids off one Friday, and I closed them myself without a word and stacked his gloves by the door. I thought of it as protecting him from the lane's opinion. In September Sharda came to the gate. Her own hives were failing, and she had noticed, she said, that ours were the only ones on the lane still growing; she asked to borrow Lucius for a week. I looked at the stacked gloves. I had been closing the lids at noon. He, I learned that evening, had been opening them again at one. Now he stands at the gate with Sharda's smoker in his hand, waiting for me to say whether he may go.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It begins with the scents of the yard, then explains the Friday custom of the lane, and ends by describing the hives again.
It begins with a request that recasts a quiet act, then explains the narrator's quiet act of control, and ends with a question left open.
It begins with the narrator's quiet act of control, then presents a request that recasts that act, and ends by resolving the dispute.
It begins with the narrator's quiet act of control, then presents a request that recasts that act, and ends with a question left open.
items.explanation: 글은 화자가 아들이 열어 둔 뚜껑을 말없이 닫고 장갑을 치워 둔 행동을 아들을 보호하는 일로 여겼다는 데서 출발한다. 이후 Sharda가 화자네 벌통만 자라고 있다며 Lucius를 빌려 달라고 요청하고, 아들이 매주 뚜껑을 다시 열어 왔다는 사실이 드러나면서 앞의 행동이 통제였음이 다시 읽힌다. 마지막은 화자가 허락할지 말지 정하지 않은 장면으로 열려 있으므로 D가 정답이다. A는 도입 묘사만 요약했고, B는 전개 순서를 뒤집었으며, C는 열린 결말을 갈등의 해결로 오독했다.

items.passage: Three chairs, two mirrors, one radio that only found the football: that was Radek's father's barbershop in Thessaloniki, where Defne and I spent every Saturday of our childhood. After my family moved to Athens, I wrote to Defne twice and then stopped. The second letter was the one in which I finally apologized for leaving without saying goodbye. Years later I came back for a funeral and walked in for a haircut. Radek, older now, ran the shop. He seated me in the middle chair and, without asking, cut my hair exactly the way his father used to, short at the back and long over the ears. I took it as kindness, a way of saying nothing had changed. When he finished, he turned the chair toward the second mirror, where a postcard-sized envelope was tucked into the frame: my own handwriting, addressed to Defne, unopened. She had left it there, he said, the week she moved away herself, in case I ever came in. I paid. I did not take the envelope down.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It begins with a gesture the narrator reads as welcome, then reveals an object that recasts that gesture, and ends without the narrator acting on it.
It begins with a list describing the shop, then recalls the narrator's childhood visits, and ends by returning to that childhood.
It begins with an object that recasts a gesture, then describes the gesture the narrator reads as welcome, and ends without the narrator acting on it.
It begins with a gesture the narrator reads as welcome, then reveals an object that recasts that gesture, and ends by repairing the old friendship.
items.explanation: 지문의 중심 장면은 Radek이 묻지도 않고 옛날 방식으로 머리를 잘라 주는 몸짓이며, 화자는 이를 아무것도 변하지 않았다는 환대로 받아들인다. 이어 거울에 꽂힌 뜯기지 않은 사과 편지가 드러나면서 그 몸짓은 화자가 뒤늦게 남긴 것을 마주하게 하는 장치로 다시 읽히고, 화자는 편지를 꺼내지 않은 채 끝난다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 도입부의 회상만 구조로 요약했고, C는 몸짓과 편지의 순서를 뒤집었으며, D는 행동하지 않는 결말을 우정의 회복으로 잘못 읽었다.

items.passage: Cleotilde and Imtiaz had played chess in the abandoned orchard outside Lyon every Sunday since the club lost its hall. __Their board sat on a stump, and the club's old rule, written on a card tucked beneath it, said that a touched piece must be moved.__ The pear trees had gone wild; fruit split on the grass and drew wasps. The two rivals spoke little, played slowly, and kept score in a notebook that neither would let the other hold. They had been trading the lead for eleven years. This Sunday a wasp landed on Imtiaz's queen. He brushed it away, and his knuckle tipped the queen onto its side. Cleotilde looked at the piece, then at the stump. Moving the queen now would cost him the game and the lead. She reached under the board, slid out the card, and folded it into her coat pocket. Then she set the queen upright on its square and waited.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It establishes the setting by showing how the two players arrange their weekly game.
It introduces a standard that later becomes the basis of a choice Cleotilde makes.
It contrasts the players' orderly game with the disorder of the wild orchard.
It explains why the two players keep score in a notebook neither will share.
items.explanation: 밑줄 문장은 단독으로 보면 그루터기 위 체스판과 카드 한 장을 묘사하는 배경 설명처럼 보인다. 그러나 후반부에 Imtiaz가 실수로 퀸을 건드려 규칙대로라면 경기를 잃게 되자, Cleotilde가 그 카드를 빼서 주머니에 넣고 퀸을 다시 세운다. 따라서 밑줄 문장은 후반의 선택을 가능하게 하는 기준을 미리 심어 둔 복선이므로 B가 정답이다. A는 밑줄 문장의 표면 기능만 읽었고, C는 바로 뒤 문장의 무성한 과수원 묘사와의 관계로만 보았으며, D는 지문의 노트 표현을 빌렸지만 후반 사건과 연결되지 않는다.

items.passage: When the season ended on Maui, the little theater on Front Street ran one film a night for whoever wandered in, and Bogdan, who had run its projector for thirty years, let Larissa sit with him in the booth. __He called her Lara, the way her grandmother had, and she let him, though no one else had used that name since the funeral.__ They watched through the small square window while the reel ticked beside them. Between shows Bogdan oiled the gears and told her which seats squeaked and which ones leaked in the rain. One night in October he asked her to thread the projector herself. Her hands shook; the film slipped twice from the sprockets. When the picture finally steadied on the screen, Bogdan took a marker from his pocket. On the strip of tape above the booth door, where his own name had been written for thirty years, he added a second name beneath it: Lara.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It portrays Bogdan as an old friend who still misses Larissa's late grandmother.
It shifts the focus from family memories to the daily work of the booth.
It prepares for a later moment in which Bogdan marks Larissa as his successor.
It suggests that Larissa puts up with old habits out of politeness to Bogdan.
items.explanation: 밑줄 문장은 단독으로 보면 Bogdan이 할머니를 그리워하며 옛 애칭을 쓰는 인물 묘사처럼 보인다. 그러나 후반부에 Larissa가 처음으로 혼자 영사기를 걸어 화면을 안정시키자, Bogdan은 자신의 이름 아래에 바로 그 애칭 'Lara'를 적어 그녀를 영사실의 후계자로 표시한다. 따라서 밑줄 문장은 그 애칭이 후반에 다른 의미를 얻도록 준비하는 복선이므로 C가 정답이다. A는 밑줄 문장의 표면만 읽었고, B는 바로 뒤 문장과의 관계로만 기능을 보았으며, D는 'let him'이라는 표현을 일반화했을 뿐 후반 사건을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: Years later, I still hear the horn of the river ferry at the Chengdu terminal, where my grandfather Haoran taught me his dialect on the waiting benches. __He made me name everything we saw, rope, gull, ticket, rain, and he corrected only my tones, never my choice of words.__ Obinna, who sold tickets at the window, had picked up some of the dialect too, and on slow afternoons he quizzed me along with Grandfather. That spring a rumor went around the terminal that my grandfather was selling his house and leaving the city. It reached Obinna before it reached me, and Obinna, meaning well, asked me in the dialect whether I would miss him. I understood every word. I answered in the dialect, tones and all. Grandfather, who had been listening from the next bench, said nothing. That evening, at home, he began teaching me the words for the things in his house, one room at a time, the stove, the clock, the drawer of letters.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It characterizes Haoran as a patient but exacting teacher of spoken tones.
It explains how Obinna came to learn the dialect alongside the narrator.
It suggests that the dialect matters more to Haoran than his house does.
It sets up the method Haoran later turns toward preserving his home in words.
items.explanation: 밑줄 문장은 단독으로 읽으면 눈에 보이는 것마다 이름을 부르게 하는 할아버지의 교수법을 소개하는 인물 묘사처럼 보인다. 그러나 할아버지가 집을 팔고 떠난다는 소문을 손녀가 방언으로 알아듣고 대답한 뒤, 그는 그날 밤부터 집 안의 물건 이름을 방마다 가르치기 시작한다. 따라서 밑줄 문장의 '이름 부르기' 방식은 후반에 떠나기 전 집을 말로 남기는 행위로 이어지는 복선이므로 D가 정답이다. A는 밑줄 문장의 표면 기능만 보았고, B는 바로 뒤 문장과의 관계로만 읽었으며, C는 지문 표현을 빌려 일반화했지만 집의 물건을 가르치는 후반 행동과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Aiko kept everything. In the harbor town in Hokkaido where we had both retired, her house held forty years of programs from the theater where we once sang duets, each one pressed flat and labeled by year. __She told me once, over tea, that she had never missed a single performance of mine, not even after we stopped singing together.__ I laughed, and she poured more tea. Her husband, Haruo, mended nets on the jetty below the house and waved whenever I passed. Last winter, after Aiko's stroke, Haruo asked me to help sort her desk. In the bottom drawer, under the programs, we found ticket stubs: one for every concert I had given alone, in Osaka, in Sapporo, in cities she had told me she had never visited. Haruo held one up to the window light. He did not ask me what it meant, and I put the stubs back in the order she had left them.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It offers a remark that the drawer's contents later show to be literally true.
It conveys a polite compliment that the narrator treats as a kind exaggeration.
It introduces the friendship that Haruo shares with the narrator in town.
It suggests that Aiko kept old records mainly out of a love of order.
items.explanation: 밑줄 문장은 단독으로 보면 오랜 동료가 건넨 인사치레 같은 말이고, 화자도 웃어넘긴다. 그러나 후반부에 서랍에서 화자가 혼자 공연한 모든 콘서트의 표가 나오면서, Aiko가 가 본 적 없다던 도시까지 몰래 찾아가 공연을 보았다는 사실이 드러난다. 따라서 밑줄 문장은 나중에 문자 그대로 사실로 밝혀지는 말을 미리 심어 둔 것이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 밑줄 문장과 화자의 웃음만 보고 표면 기능을 골랐고, C는 바로 뒤 문장의 Haruo 소개와의 관계로만 보았으며, D는 'kept everything'을 빌려 일반화했을 뿐 서랍의 발견을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: I run a spice shop in Marrakesh that a former ship's cook built to look like a galley, all brass hooks and low beams, and every morning Joaquin ducks under those beams to complain about my saffron. Too damp, too pale, too expensive. He has said this for nine years. He buys a gram each time anyway, counted out of a jar he insists I lift down from the top shelf. Last month a hotel offered to buy my stock and the lease; I could retire to my daughter's house in Fes. I told Joaquin, mostly to watch his face. He said good, the hotel's saffron would at least be dry. I am not saying I was hurt, exactly. I signed nothing that week. I did move the jar to the lowest shelf, where a man with a bad back could reach it himself, and I wrote the price on the lid in larger numbers.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Joaquin?
options: Weary irritation at his complaints while hoping the sale will put an end to them
Real fondness for him while feeling guilty about nearly selling the shop
Protective care for him while keeping up a show of mutual grumbling
Proud attachment to the galley shop while doubting its worth to customers
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 화자는 Joaquin의 불평을 건조하게 옮기고 그의 반응을 보려고 매각 이야기를 꺼내는 등 서로 투덜대는 말투를 유지한다. 중간의 'not saying I was hurt, exactly'라는 망설이는 정정은 그 말투 아래 감정이 있음을 암시한다. 뒤에서 화자는 아무것도 서명하지 않고, 허리가 아픈 Joaquin이 직접 닿도록 병을 아래 칸으로 옮기며 가격을 크게 적는데, 이는 그를 배려하는 행동이다. 따라서 C가 정답이며, A는 말투만 읽었고, B는 배려의 이유를 죄책감으로 바꾸었으며, D는 지문의 가게 묘사를 빌려 태도로 일반화했다.

items.passage: Kaya had interpreted for Nneka for three years, and she would tell anyone who asked that the woman was impossible. Nneka changed her mind mid-sentence, made Kaya repeat whole contracts twice, and insisted, every Friday after their meetings, on stopping at the same shoe repair stall in Lagos to have the same left heel glued. The heel did not need gluing. Kaya said so, in two languages, to Nneka and to the cobbler. Neither listened. She would not have called the Fridays pleasant, not quite. Last week Nneka's company assigned a new interpreter, a young man with excellent references, and Nneka mentioned it in the car as though discussing the weather. Kaya said nothing. On Friday she went to the stall early, alone, paid the cobbler in advance for a month of heels, and left the receipt with Nneka's name on it.
items.question: Which choice best describes Kaya's attitude toward Nneka, as conveyed in the text?
options: Lasting exasperation with Nneka while doubting the new interpreter's skill
Warm attachment to Nneka while acting from guilt over past complaints
Dry amusement at the heel repairs while dismissing them as wasted money
Quiet devotion to their shared habit while voicing steady complaint about it
items.explanation: 앞부분의 Kaya는 Nneka를 '불가능한 사람'이라 말하고 굽 수리가 필요 없다고 두 언어로 불평한다. 중간의 'not pleasant, not quite'라는 망설이는 정정은 그 불평이 전부가 아님을 암시한다. 자신이 교체된다는 소식 뒤에도 Kaya는 혼자 가게에 가 한 달 치 굽 수리비를 미리 내고 Nneka 이름으로 영수증을 남기는데, 이는 함께해 온 금요일 습관을 지키려는 행동이다. 따라서 D가 정답이며, A는 말투만 읽었고, B는 애정의 이유를 죄책감으로 바꾸었으며, C는 지문의 굽 수리 표현을 빌려 불평 쪽으로만 일반화했다.

items.passage:
Two rules for the crossing at the dry riverbed in Vermont:
step on the flat stones, and do not mention the trial.
Solange, retired from the bench, keeps the first rule loudly;
she lectures me on stones the way she once lectured juries,
and I roll my eyes behind her, as clerks are allowed to do.
Her rulings ran long. So do her walks.
I would not call this friendship, exactly.
The second rule we keep without a word.
Last week, halfway across, she slowed
where the old flood line still stains the bank,
the place where the case began.
I started talking about stones,
the gray ones, the split ones, the one shaped like a gavel,
and kept on talking until we reached the far side,
and offered my arm for the climb, which she took.
items.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward Solange?
options: Protective loyalty toward her while keeping up a show of mild mockery
Mild impatience with her while enduring her lectures out of duty
Real respect for her while feeling guilty about the old trial
Fond interest in the stones while ignoring the flood line on the bank
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 화자는 Solange의 돌 강의에 뒤에서 눈을 굴리고 그녀의 판결과 산책이 길다고 농담하며 가벼운 조롱의 말투를 쓴다. 중간의 'not friendship, exactly'라는 망설이는 정정은 그 말투 아래 다른 감정이 있음을 암시한다. 뒤에서 Solange가 사건이 시작된 홍수선 앞에서 걸음을 늦추자 화자는 일부러 돌 이야기를 끝까지 이어 가고 팔을 내밀어 그녀를 지킨다. 따라서 A가 정답이며, B는 말투만 읽었고, C는 배려의 이유를 화자의 죄책감으로 바꾸었으며, D는 지문의 돌과 홍수선 표현을 빌렸을 뿐 화자의 의도를 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: Years later, I still poke fun at my mother-in-law about the report. I had been married to Friedrich for two months and teaching gymnastics at a Vienna school for three when Alonso, a ten-year-old, slipped off the low beam and broke his wrist while I was on duty. My mother-in-law, once a headmistress, arrived that evening with a red pen and a terrible opinion of my commas. She crossed out "momentarily distracted" and wrote "I was looking at another student." She crossed out "unfortunate fall" and wrote "he fell." I called her a tyrant that night, and I still do, at holidays, to make Friedrich laugh. I would not say I enjoyed the evening, not exactly. Every report I have written since sits in a folder on my desk, and before I submit one, I read it aloud once in her flat, slow voice, red pen in hand.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward her mother-in-law?
options: Lingering annoyance at her while doubting the fairness of her edits
Lasting respect for her while maintaining a playful show of grievance
Lasting respect for her while still ashamed of Alonso's injury
Amused regard for her commas while doubting their value in reports
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 화자는 시어머니를 놀리고 '폭군'이라 부르며 쉼표에 대한 그녀의 '끔찍한 의견'을 불평하는 농담조를 쓴다. 중간의 'not enjoyed, not exactly'라는 망설이는 정정은 그 불평이 진심의 전부가 아님을 암시한다. 뒤에서 화자는 지금도 보고서를 제출하기 전에 그녀의 목소리로 소리 내어 읽고 빨간 펜을 드는데, 이는 정직하게 쓰는 법을 가르쳐 준 그녀를 깊이 존중한다는 행동 단서다. 따라서 B가 정답이며, A는 말투만 읽었고, C는 존중의 이유를 사고에 대한 수치심으로 바꾸었으며, D는 지문의 쉼표 표현을 빌려 일반화했다.
